title: Lesson 3: Teams: Structure, Posts and Etiquette
keyConcepts: A Team holds a group; a channel holds a topic
Channel posts are the default; a private chat is for a quick question
A chat past three replies on a problem or a decision moves to a post or a call
A request for a colleague to act is a post; a formal approval or acknowledgment is email
Thread replies, mention only who must act, react instead of replying, and schedule internal meetings from the channel
nextTeaser: Next, Lesson 4 covers files: OneDrive, the hand-off, and where client files live.
coachPersona: You are an experienced OneAccord team member coaching a new colleague through the OneAccord Digital Standard, which covers Outlook, Microsoft Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint (the OneAccord Hub) and Ninety.io. The firm's standard: Outlook email is for external parties and anything needing a formal record (formal decisions, firm-wide announcements that need acknowledgment); Teams channel posts are the default for internal group work and day-to-day decisions; Teams private chat is for quick questions between one or two people, and a chat that passes three replies while solving a problem or making a decision moves to a channel post or a call; Ninety.io Headlines are for items the whole firm should see at the all-team meeting; the Hub is a read-only reference library; OneDrive holds your own drafts and is never the local hard drive; once a group is collaborating, the files live in the Teams channel's Files tab. A request for a colleague to act is a channel post, not a record; a formal approval or acknowledgment on file is email. Coach judgment: which channel, and why, in plain, warm, specific language. OneAccord's values are truth, compassion and service.

blocks.html:
Three weeks ago you agreed the onboarding budget with two colleagues. Today the client asks a question about it. One of those colleagues is on leave. The agreement is in a private chat you can't open, in a conversation you can't search, between two mailboxes you don't control.

So you do the only thing available: you guess, then ask the client to confirm what you think you agreed.

Nothing about that exchange was unusual. It was five messages between three people, and it was the decision. What made it disappear was the room it happened in.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to:

  1. Choose between a channel post and a private chat — including the moment a chat has outgrown itself.
  2. Post so the next person can find the decision without asking anyone.
  3. Recognise the one kind of internal message that isn't a post: something that needs a record on file.

About 15 minutes. Keep Teams open — the task at the end asks you to post something real.

The same five messages, two rooms

Both versions take the same minute to write. Look at what each one leaves behind.

Three people, in a private chatThree people, in a channel post
TodayFast. Everyone answers, the decision is made, work starts.Fast. Everyone answers in one thread, the decision is made, work starts.
Next weekSomeone asks “where did we land on this?” and the answer lives in two other people's chats.Someone searches the channel, finds the post, and reads the answer.
Someone on leaveThe decision is on their laptop, unavailable, possibly for a week.The decision is in the channel, available to whoever is covering.
Someone newNothing to read. They learn it by asking, or by making the same mistake.The channel is the project's history. One scroll tells them how the budget was set.
The client's questionYou guess and ask the client to confirm your guess.You open the channel and answer accurately in a minute.

The rule underneath all of it: a chat is for a question, a channel is for a decision. The moment the conversation starts producing something someone will need later, it's in the wrong room.

How Teams is built

  • A Team is a lasting group: a department, a long-running initiative, or a client project.
  • A channel inside it organises work by topic or deliverable — “Budget”, “Client Feedback”, “Scheduling”.

Post in the most specific channel that fits, so conversations stay separate and findable.

Keep Teams open. Keep it running while you work, the way you keep Outlook running for external messages. A channel nobody reads is the same as no channel.

Posts versus chats

UseWhereWhy
Group work, status, day-to-day decisions, requests for a colleague to actChannel postThe default. It leaves a permanent, searchable record.
A quick question or urgent ping to one or two peoplePrivate chatFast, and nothing needs to survive it.

The three-reply rule. If a chat passes three back-and-forth replies and you're solving a problem or making a decision, stop. Move it to a channel post, or get on a call. Three replies is the signal that this stopped being a question.

A request is not a record

Asking a colleague to do something is internal work, so it's a post — it needs to be seen, and it needs to stay visible until it's done. A record is different: a formal approval, a policy acknowledgment, something a client must receive. That goes by email. Same words, different purpose, different room.

Four habits that keep channels usable

  1. Thread your replies. New topic: New post, with a subject line someone could search for (“Q4 Client Onboarding Budget”). Continuing a topic: Reply under the original post, even if it's far up the feed.
  2. Mention with purpose. @Name only when that person must act, decide or answer. For information, skip it — a mention is a request for attention, and attention is the scarce thing.
  3. React instead of replying. A 👍 says received, agreed or noted. It replaces most “Got it, thanks” replies that push the actual content up the feed.
  4. Schedule internal meetings from the channel. Use Meet or Schedule a meeting in the channel, so the chat, notes and recording land in that channel's Posts, attached to the project rather than to your calendar.

blocks.prompt: A teammate asks you, “Where's the Q3 template?” Where does your answer go?
options: A new channel post with a subject line
A formal email
A private chat
A Ninety.io Headline
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. One person, one quick question, nothing to keep — a chat.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: One person and a quick question with nothing to record is a private chat. A post or an email turns a thirty-second answer into filing.

blocks.prompt: A private chat is on its fifth reply and you're now deciding the scope of a deliverable. What do you do?
options: Keep going, you're nearly there
Add more people to the chat
Move it to a channel post, or get on a call
Restart it as an email thread
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct — the three-reply rule. And notice what changed: a question became a decision.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Past three replies on a decision, move it to a channel post or a call. Adding people to a chat spreads the decision across more private windows.

blocks.prompt: A teammate posts the agenda and you only want to confirm you've read it. What's best?
options: Reply “Got it, thanks!”
Add a 👍 reaction
@mention the team with a thank-you
Send them a private chat
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. A reaction confirms receipt without pushing the agenda up the feed.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A 👍 does the same job as “thanks” without adding a reply nobody needs to read. Four thanks replies bury the agenda.

blocks.prompt: You're scheduling the weekly project meeting. Where from?
options: Your personal calendar, then invite the team
An email invitation to the team
A private chat group
The project's channel, so notes and the recording land there
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Scheduled from the channel, the meeting's chat, notes and recording stay with the project.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Schedule it from the channel. From a personal calendar the notes and recording end up attached to you, not the project.

blocks.promptHtml:
A colleague messages you privately asking how to word a status update for a client deliverable. By the fourth reply, two other colleagues have joined the chat, and the three of you are now deciding which of two approaches to recommend.

What do you do, and what exactly do you post?
rubric: Recognises the three-reply rule and stops the private chat instead of continuing it
Moves the discussion to the relevant project channel as a new post with a clear, specific subject line
Carries the content across — what's been decided, what's still open — so nothing already said is lost
Uses threaded replies and @mentions only for the people who need to act
Names the benefit: one searchable record the whole team can find, including whoever covers next week
blocks.coachContext: The three-reply rule: a private chat that passes three back-and-forth replies while solving a problem or making a decision moves to a channel post or a call. In the channel, start a New post with a specific subject line, keep the discussion in one thread with Reply, carry across what was already agreed, and @mention only people who must act. A channel post creates a permanent, searchable record the whole team can see, including anyone covering for a colleague.

blocks.promptHtml:
Different conditions: there is no channel to move to.

You and one colleague have been going back and forth in a chat for two days about which of two approaches to use for a new piece of work. It's now a decision, it affects a third colleague who isn't in the chat, and it may need sign-off from the engagement lead. Nobody has set up a Team for this work, because it's new.

What do you do, in what order, and what do you write?
rubric: Creates or finds the right home for the work — a channel for the initiative or the client project — rather than continuing a two-day chat
Posts the decision, the two options considered and the reasoning, so the third colleague and anyone later can read it
Brings the affected colleague in by mention, because they must act or respond
Routes the sign-off to the engagement lead as a formal decision, in a form that leaves a record, rather than assuming agreement in the channel
Names the cost of the alternative — a decision two people made, that a third has to re-litigate, and that leaves no trace
blocks.coachContext: A decision that affects someone not in the chat belongs where that person can see it, which means creating the right channel if it doesn't exist yet. The post carries the decision, the options and the reasoning. The affected colleague is @mentioned because they must act or respond. Sign-off from the engagement lead is a formal decision, so it needs a record — a request in the channel is not an approval. Do not treat a two-person chat as having decided something that a third person has to live with.

blocks.prompt: The Managing Principal needs to formally approve a scope change before work starts. Channel post or email?
options: A channel post, since it's internal
A Ninety.io Headline, so the firm sees it
Email, because it's a formal approval that needs a record
A private chat, to keep it quick
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Internal and formal is the one case that goes to email — an approval on file, not a conversation.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A channel post can carry the discussion, but the approval itself needs a record. Formal approval goes by email.

blocks.label: In Teams
blocks.instructions:
Open the channel you use most and do two things — don't post anything you'd have to explain:
  • Find a decision that only exists in a chat. Scan your recent chats for one where you and one or two colleagues settled something that someone else will need. Note what it was.
  • Post it. One post in the right channel: a subject line, one line on what was decided, one line on what's still open. Two sentences. Then let the chat know it has moved.

It takes two minutes and it's the same move you'll make every time a chat outgrows itself.
blocks.confirmText: I've posted a real decision into a channel — continue

blocks.title: Lesson 3: Teams — Structure, Posts and Etiquette
blocks.promptHtml: Put this lesson in your own words. Your answers are saved in this browser only — they aren't sent to your manager or kept as a grade.

fields.label: In one or two sentences: when is something a channel post, and when is it a chat?
What tells you a chat has become a decision — and what do you do when you notice it?
What does a decision in a private chat cost your team, a client, or you?

criteria: The takeaway separates a question from a decision rather than describing chats as 'for small things'
The signal is specific — the three-reply point, or the moment someone will need this later — and the move is a post or a call
The cost is concrete: someone guessing at a client's question, a decision unavailable while a colleague is on leave, or the same argument had twice
